name: Buluba-Lulua
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 5 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Morrison, W. M. 1906. Grammar and dictionary of the Buluba-Lulua language as spoken in the Upper Kasai and Congo Basin. New York: American Tract Society.
catalog_locator: Part I (Orthography), IV. Accent, sec. 35, p. 10 (archive.org item grammardictionar00morr, page scan leaf n23; djvu scanned text)
catalog_quote: 35. As a general rule it may be said that the accent in simple words falls on the penult with also a secondary accent on the fourth syllable from the end in polysyllabic words. In inflected words the accent is on the initial syllable of the root; when more than two syllables follow the accented syllable a secondary accent falls on the penult. But it must be constantly borne in mind that Buluba-Lulua words are, for the most part, devoid of a strong accent on any syllable. In this respect this language resembles the French. The smoothness of pronunciation and the lack of strong accent make it all the more difficult for English-speaking persons to refrain from giving too much accent to the words, since the English has such decided accent on all words of more than one syllable. ... Citékutéku, greens; bakufúndilangána, they have written to each other. Rem. -Diphthongs, of course, are regard…
sweep_summary: search for luba1249 (Luba-Lulua, in catalog as 'morphological' on Morrison 1906 §35) had one title item: Weier 1992, Tonrelationen in Luba-Sprichwörtern (Köppe, x+272 pp, German). Publisher record and abstract (saved; updated) show it is a study of tonal rhyme patterns (H/T sequences, tonal end-rhyme, chiasmus, reversivity) in Cilubà proverbs — prosody of verbal art built on tone, not word-stress placement. No open copy exists (Google Books id 8nwOAAAAYAAJ no preview; not on HathiTrust or archive.org; PDF sold by Köppe); relevance 'prosody-but-not-word-stress', access abstract-only, priority low.org (WorldCat, JSTOR, DNB blocked). Best first-hand stress statement remains Stappers 1949 p.4 + fn.1 (held held by the project from the 9/16 check and re-read now): dynamic accent evenly distributed, subordinate to length and tone; general rule penult, audible only in words of 4+ syllables — which supersedes Morrison 1906 as deciding source and supports the pending reclassify as 'tonal / weak penult' rather than 'morphological'. Nothing in this search of works with stress in the title changes that recommendation.

new_statements.quote: a. Het dynamisch accent (ademdruk). — De ademdruk wordt zo gelijkmatig over de klankgrepen verdeeld, dat het met het gehoor alleen moeilijk is uit te maken waar de intensiteitstoppen liggen. Maar ongetwijfeld is dit accent als structurele factor van ondergeschikt belang in vergelijking met de lengte en de toonhoogte. [fn.1:] Vgl. B, nr. 34. Een onderzoek ter plaatse wijst uit dat het dynamisch accent om tegenstelling of nadruk aan te geven gemakkelijk vast te stellen is. Ook voor de rhythmische functie is het mogelijk de plaats van het dyn. acc. aan te wijzen op gehoor alleen, doch alleen in woorden die meer dan drie klankgrepen tellen, valt het aanstonds op. De algemene regel is: op de voorlaatste klankgreep.
new_statements.translation: a. The dynamic accent (breath pressure). — Breath pressure is distributed so evenly over the syllables that by ear alone it is hard to determine where the intensity peaks lie. But undoubtedly this accent is, as a structural factor, of subordinate importance compared with length and pitch. [fn.1:] Cf. Burssens [1939], no. 34. Field investigation shows that the dynamic accent used to mark contrast or emphasis is easy to establish. For the rhythmic function too it is possible to locate the dynamic accent by ear alone, but only in words of more than three syllables is it immediately noticeable. The general rule is: on the penultimate syllable.
new_statements.citation: Stappers, Leo (met medewerking van Em. Willems). 1949. Tonologische bijdrage tot de studie van het werkwoord in het Tshiluba. (Institut Royal Colonial Belge, Section des Sciences Morales et Politiques, Mémoires in-8°, XVIII/4.) Bruxelles. 188 pp.
new_statements.locator: Inleidende begrippen §3, p.4 with footnote 1 (PDF page 19)
new_statements.reading: Tone language; dynamic stress is weak, non-culminative and structurally subordinate to vowel length and tone; where a rhythmic stress is audible at all (words of 4+ syllables) it falls on the PENULT. No support for Morrison's root-initial accent in inflected words (what is stem-bound in Stappers/Wils is contrastive vowel length, 'stamaccent' = quantity). This is the same passage already flagged in the reclassify queue ( line 149: 'penultimate, weak/non-dominant (tone language)'); the Weier title item adds nothing to it.

new_statements.second_reader_bearing_note: Same finding, one ordering refinement: lead with 'tonal / no dominant word stress' rather than 'penultimate'. Stappers 1949 p.4 ranks dynamic accent as structurally subordinate to length and tone and audible only in words of more than three syllables; the penult rule is a footnote about rhythmic prominence, with the promised fuller account never given in the book. So: classification tonal (not in the dominant set); caution/the primary-stress rule = weak rhythmic penult in 4+-syllable words, contrastive vowel length stem-bound (Stappers's 'stamaccent' is quantity, not stress); drop 'morphologi…

tone_statements.citation: Hulstaert, Gustaaf. 1941. Tonetiek van Lomongo en Tshiluba. Aequatoria 4: 56-58. (Coquilhatville.) [whole volume 4 online:https://www.aequatoria.be/publications/assets/Aequatoria_1941.pdf]
tone_statements.quote: De algemeene uitkomst van de vergelijking tusschen lɔmɔngɔ en tshiluba op tonetisch gebied is dat de tonen in beide talen gansch tegenovergesteld zijn aan elkaar. Met andere woorden: al wat in het lɔmɔngɔ hoogtonig is, is in het tshiluba laagtonig, en omgekeerd. … In het lɔmɔngɔ zijn de naamwoordelijke prefixen steeds laag, in het tshiluba zijn ze hoog … Het koppelwoord is hoog in het praesens in tshiluba (dí) en laag in het lɔmɔngɔ (le). … Het bezits-partikel a is in het tshiluba laag, doch hoog in het enkelvoud der klassen mu-ba en n-n.
tone_statements.translation: The general result of the comparison between Lomongo and Tshiluba in the tonetic domain is that the tones in the two languages are entirely opposite to each other. In other words: everything that is high-toned in Lomongo is low-toned in Tshiluba, and vice versa. ... In Lomongo the nominal prefixes are always low, in Tshiluba they are high ... The copula is high in the present in Tshiluba (dí) and low in Lomongo (le). ... The possessive particle a is low in Tshiluba, but high in the singular of the classes mu-ba and n-n.
tone_statements.locator: p. 56, right column (continued p. 57 with the word-pair table)
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Comparative note: Tshiluba has high and low tones, the reverse of Lomongo cognates (noun prefixes high, copula dí high, possessive a low); word pairs after Burssens; two tones implied, not counted.

tone_statements.citation: Burssens, Amaat F. S. 1939. Le luba, langue à intonation, et le tambour-signal. In: Proceedings of the Third International Congress of Phonetic Sciences, held at the University of Ghent, 18-22 July 1938, 503-507. Ghent: Laboratory of Phonetics of the University.
tone_statements.quote: Luba, langue bantoue, est une langue a intonation, présentant deuX tons fondamentaux, l’un aigu (ton haut, a), l’autre gra‘ve (ton has, a), et deux tons composes, l’un descendant (a < a +‘a), l’autre ascendant (a < a + a). Le tfiLﬁb‘a du Kasai possede en outre un ton secondaire moyen (a). Dans une langue a intonation, telle que le Luba, toutes les syllabes présentent entre elles des intervalles musicaux. Chaque syllabe doit étre prononcée sur un certain ton; l’intonation de la syllabe, 1a mélodie du mot dans la phrase détermment 1a signiﬁcation du mot ou sa fonction grammaticale.
tone_statements.translation: Luba, a Bantu language, is a tone language, presenting two fundamental tones, one acute (high tone, á), the other grave (low tone, à), and two compound tones, one falling (â < á + à), the other rising (ǎ < à + á). The Tshiluba of Kasai has in addition a secondary mid tone. In a tone language such as Luba, all the syllables present musical intervals between them. Each syllable must be pronounced on a certain tone; the intonation of the syllable, the melody of the word in the sentence, determine the meaning of the word or its grammatical function.
tone_statements.summary: Two fundamental tones, high and low, on every syllable, lexical and grammatical; falling and rising are compounds of the two; Kasai Tshiluba adds a secondary mid tone. Nothing on word stress.

audit.recode_to: penultimate, weak/non-dominant (tone language; dynamic stress evenly distributed, audible only in words of 4+ syllables, general rule penult; contrastive length stem-bound) — citing Stappers 1949 p.4 + fn.1 alongside Morrison 1906 §35; confirm against Burssens 1939 §34 before finalising. At minimum add a caution and drop 'morphological' as the headline class.
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: Morrison 1906 §35 p.10 is verbatim in both the scanned text we hold and the page scan we hold; locator correct. (2) Deciding source: a 1906 missionary learner's grammar-dictionary; its own text hedges that words are 'for the most part devoid of a strong accent'. Glottolog and the local sources.bib list a deep specialist prosodic literature for Luba-Kasai (Burssens 1939, Stappers 1949, Coupez 1954, Maddieson 1976, Lukusa 1993/1997, Yukawa 1992, De Schryver 1999, Bostoen 1999/2003) that the record ignores, so Morrison is not the best available description. (3) downloaded now (open): Stappers 1949 (KAOW-ARSOM digitised memoir), a 188-pp tonological monograph on the Tshiluba verb, states on p.4 that dynamic accent is spread so evenly that intensity peaks are hard to locate by ear, is structurally subordinate to length and tone, and — fn.1, citing Burssens 1939 §34 and his own fieldwork

ACCENT' sec. 35 is verbatim in the the scanned text we hold) and in the page scan we hold, which I re-read: penult in simple words (+ secondary on 4th-from-end), root-initial in inflected words (+ secondary penult), then the italicised hedge 'But it must be constantly borne in mind that Buluba-Lulua words are, for the most part, devoid of a strong accent on any syllable', examples Citékutéku, bakufúndilangána, and after the Rem. on diphthongs: Kúdua, kúnua, kúdia, káhia, kubué

sources.quote: Publisher abstract (English, verbatim): 'This study tries to elaborate a structure principle for proverbs. The basis therefore is given in the present tonality of the (Ci-)Luba language (C.31). Tonal rhyme relations are identifiable with argument comparison ... Complete tonal iteration proves the simple tone parallelism already described by Stappers, partial iteration is depending on position, and leads to additional, now defineable tonal rhyme patterns in proverbs. They deal with initial, internal, ending, and external rhymes as well as with tonal chain alignment and chiasmus.' Review (Kabuta, Anthropos 91/1996: 314f.): 'Le grand mérite de l'ouvrage de Weier est de mettre en évidence l'existence de structures tonales précises, qui se superposent à cette structure sémantico-syntaxique'.
